On some log-concavity properties of the Alexander-Conway and Links-Gould invariantsThanks:  Key words and phrases: Links–Gould invariant, Alexander polynomial, alternating links, unimodality, log-concavity, Lorentzian polynomials.

Matthew Harper Address: Michigan State University, East Lansing, Michigan, USA Email address: mrhmath@proton.me , Ben-Michael Kohli Address: Section de Mathématiques, Université de Genève
rue du Conseil-Général 7-9, 1205 Genève, Switzerland Email address: bm.kohli@protonmail.ch , Jiebo Song Address: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Huairou District, Beijing, China Email address: songjiebo@bimsa.cn and Guillaume Tahar Address: Beijing Institute of Mathematical Sciences and Applications, Huairou District, Beijing, China Email address: guillaume.tahar@bimsa.cn
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The Links–Gould invariant LG⁡(L,t0,t1)\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1}) of a link LL is a two-variable quantum generalization of the Alexander–Conway polynomial ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t) and has been shown to share some of its most geometric features in several recent works. Here we suggest that LG\mathrm{LG} likely shares another of the Alexander polynomial’s most distinctive - and mysterious - properties: for alternating links, the coefficients of the Links-Gould polynomial alternate and appear to form a log-concave two-indexed sequence with no internal zeros. The former was observed by Ishii for knots with up to 10 crossings. We further conjecture that they satisfy a bidimensional property of unimodality, thereby replicating a long-standing conjecture of Fox (1962) regarding the Alexander polynomial, and a subsequent refinement by Stoimenow. We also point out that the Stoimenow conjecture reflects a more structural phenomenon: after a suitable normalization, the Alexander polynomial of an alternating link appears to be a Lorentzian polynomial. We give compelling experimental and computational evidence for these different properties.

1. Introduction

1.1. The Alexander and Links-Gould polynomials of links

The Alexander polynomial ΔL\Delta_{L} is an isotopy invariant of links LL valued in ℤ⁡[t±1]\mathbbm{Z}[t^{\pm 1}] and defined up to units. It was first defined in 1928 by James Waddell Alexander [Ale28] and was the first polynomial invariant of knots. Remarkably, the Alexander polynomial remained the only known polynomial link invariant until Vaughan Jones discovered his eponymous polynomial half a century later [Jon85]. Designed to distinguish links up to isotopy, the Alexander polynomial also relates to some fundamental geometric properties of knots and links. For example, the degree of ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t) is a lower bound for the 3-genus of LL [Sei35], and the Alexander polynomial of a fibered knot is monic [Neu65, Rap60, Sta61]. The Alexander invariant is also relevant to study the four-dimensional properties of a knot. For example, for a topologically slice knot KK, ΔK​(t)\Delta_{K}(t) takes a particular form known as the Fox-Milnor condition [FM66].

It is also worth noting that ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t) can be constructed as a quantum link invariant, that is, a Reshetikhin–Turaev-type invariant where it occurs in its palindromic normalization as the Alexander–Conway polynomial. It arises in this way by considering representations of either: the Hopf algebra Uq​𝔰​𝔩​(2)U_{q}{\mathfrak{sl}(2)} at fourth roots of unity, or the Hopf superalgebra Uq​𝔤​𝔩​(1|1)U_{q}\mathfrak{gl}(1|1), see [Mur92, Vir06]. In the latter perspective, the Alexander polynomial is the first in the family of Links–Gould invariants LGm,n​(L,t0,t1)∈ℤ⁡[t0±1,t1±1]\mathrm{LG}^{m,n}(L;t_{0},t_{1})\in\mathbb{Z}[t_{0}^{\pm 1},t_{1}^{\pm 1}] obtained from the Reshetikhin–Turaev construction applied to representations of the Hopf superalgebras Uq​𝔤​𝔩​(m|n)U_{q}\mathfrak{gl}(m|n), see [LG92, DWLK99, DW01]. The simplest case after the Alexander polynomial is derived from Uq​𝔤​𝔩​(2|1)U_{q}\mathfrak{gl}(2|1). We shall denote the associated invariant LG2,1\mathrm{LG}^{2,1} by LG\mathrm{LG} and refer to it as the Links–Gould polynomial.

Although LG\mathrm{LG} is not yet known to have a classical geometric interpretation that would relate it even more closely to the Alexander polynomial, recent results show that it reproduces some of the Alexander polynomial’s most distinctive characteristics. Specifically, the degree of the Links–Gould polynomial gives a lower bound for the genus of a knot by work of two of the authors [KT]. Also, the LG\mathrm{LG} invariant of a fibered link is ℤ⁡[q±1]\mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]-monic following the recent work of López-Neumann and van der Veen [LNvdV]. These two properties imply and improve upon similar statements for the Alexander polynomial. This is because LG⁡(L,t0,t1)\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1}) specializes to ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t) in at least two different ways [DWIL05, Koh16, KPM17]:

LG⁡(L,t0,−t0−1)=ΔL​(t02),LG⁡(L,t0,t0−1)=ΔL​(t0)2.\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},-t_{0}^{-1})=\Delta_{L}(t_{0}^{2})\,,\qquad\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{0}^{-1})=\Delta_{L}(t_{0})^{2}. (1)

It is therefore reasonable to imagine that other properties of the Alexander polynomial should have their counterparts for the Links-Gould invariant.

1.2. The Alexander polynomial of alternating links

A class where the Alexander polynomial has an interesting behavior is that of alternating links: the Alexander polynomial of an alternating link is alternating with no internal zeros by works of Crowell [Cro59] and Murasugi [Mur58]. This means that if we consider the Conway normalization of ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t), we can write:

ΔL​(t)=∑k=−nnak​tk,with ​al⋅al+1<0​ for all ​l∈[[−(n−1),n−1]].\Delta_{L}(t)=\sum_{k=-n}^{n}a_{k}t^{k},\quad\text{with }a_{l}\cdot a_{l+1}<0\text{ for all }l\in[\![-(n-1),n-1]\!]\,.

Moreover, Fox conjectured that the absolute values of the coefficients of the Alexander polynomial of an alternating link form a unimodal sequence [Fox61], i.e.

|a−n|≤|a−n+1|≤⋯≤|ak|=|ak+1|=⋯=|am|≥|am+1|≥⋯≥|an|​, −n≤k≤m≤n.|a_{-n}|\leq|a_{-n+1}|\leq\cdots\leq|a_{k}|=|a_{k+1}|=\cdots=|a_{m}|\geq|a_{m+1}|\geq\cdots\geq|a_{n}|\text{, }-n\leq k\leq m\leq n\,.

Stoimenow refined the statement by conjecturing that the sequence should be log-concave with no internal zeros [Sto05]. This in turn would imply that the sequence is trapezoidal:

|a−n|<|a−n+1|<⋯<|ak|=|ak+1|=⋯=|am|>|am+1|>⋯>|an|​, −n≤k≤m≤n.|a_{-n}|<|a_{-n+1}|<\cdots<|a_{k}|=|a_{k+1}|=\cdots=|a_{m}|>|a_{m+1}|>\cdots>|a_{n}|\text{, }-n\leq k\leq m\leq n\,.

Different forms of the Fox conjecture have been proved over the years for many infinite families of knots and links, see [Par78, Har79, Mur85, OS03, Jon10, Sto16, AC21, HMV24, AJK, KMP]. A summary of these studies and their scope can be found in [AJK]. It also includes several recent works [AC21, HMV24, AJK, KMP]. The general conjecture, however, remains unsolved to this day.

1.3. Similar properties for the Links-Gould polynomial of alternating links?

In his early foundational studies on the Links-Gould invariant, Ishii conjectured that LG\mathrm{LG} displays the same “alternating” behavior as the Alexander polynomial on alternating knots.

Conjecture 1.1 ([Ish06]).

The LG polynomial LG⁡(K,t0,t1)=∑i,jai​j​t0i​t1j\mathrm{LG}(K;t_{0},t_{1})=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}t_{0}^{i}t_{1}^{j} of an alternating knot KK is “alternating”: ai​j​ai′​j′≥0if ​i+j−i′−j′​ is even, andai​j​ai′​j′≤0otherwisea_{ij}a_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\geq 0\quad\text{if }i+j-i^{\prime}-j^{\prime}\text{ is even, and}\quad a_{ij}a_{i^{\prime}j^{\prime}}\leq 0\quad\text{otherwise}.

Ishii verified Conjecture 1.1 for all prime knots with up to 1010 crossings. Using the fact that LG\mathrm{LG} is equivalent by a change of variables to the Garoufalidis–Kashaev V1V_{1}-polynomial of links [GK, GHK+c, GHK+a], the computations of Garoufalidis–Li for V1V_{1} show that the Ishii conjecture is true for all prime knots with up to 1616 crossings, see [GL].

In this work we conjecture that once again the Links-Gould invariant LG\mathrm{LG} and the Alexander polynomial follow similar patterns. First, Conjecture 1.1 can be made more precise, echoing the behavior of the Alexander polynomial.

Definition 1.2.

A two-indexed sequence (ai​j)i,j∈ℤ(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{Z}} is said to have no interior zeros if

Conv​(Supp​(ai​j))∩ℤ2=Supp​(ai​j),\text{Conv}(\text{Supp}(a_{ij}))\cap\mathbb{Z}^{2}=\text{Supp}(a_{ij})\,,

where Supp​(ai​j)={(i,j)∈ℤ2:ai​j≠0}\text{Supp}(a_{ij})=\{(i,j)\in\mathbb{Z}^{2}\,:\,a_{ij}\neq 0\} and Conv​(X)\text{Conv}(X) is the convex hull of a subset XX of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}.

Conjecture 1.3 (strong version of the Ishii conjecture).

The LG polynomial LG⁡(L,t0,t1)=∑i,jai​j​t0i​t1j\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1})=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}t_{0}^{i}t_{1}^{j} of an alternating link LL with μ\mu components is “alternating” with

ai​j=(−1)μ+i+j+1​|ai​j|a_{ij}=(-1)^{\mu+i+j+1}\,|a_{ij}|

for all i,ji,j. Moreover, (ai​j)(a_{ij}) has no interior zeros.

Remark 1.4.

Conjecture 1.3 is not true for other two-variable generalizations of the Alexander polynomial, i.e. for the two variable polynomial invariant Δ𝔰​𝔩3\Delta_{\mathfrak{sl}_{3}} derived from representations of Uq​𝔰​𝔩3U_{q}\mathfrak{sl}_{3} at a fourth root of unity, studied by one of the authors [Har, Figure 10].

We further propose that LG\mathrm{LG} should satisfy bidimensional properties of log-concavity and unimodality, thereby generalizing, at least in spirit, the Fox and Stoimenow conjectures.

Definition 1.5.

A sequence (ai)i∈ℤ(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is log-concave if, for every i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, we have: ai−1​ai+1≤ai2a_{i-1}\,a_{i+1}\leq a_{i}^{2}.

Remark 1.6.

Log-concavity, as well as its generalizations we will define hereafter, is invariant under multiplication by a monomial.

Definition 1.7.

We will refer to a bidimensional sequence (ai​j)i,j∈ℤ(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{Z}} as 2d log-concave if for every i,j,k,l∈ℤi,j,k,l\in\mathbb{Z} :

ai+k,j+l​ai−k,j−l≤ai​j2.a_{i+k,j+l}\,a_{i-k,j-l}\leq a_{ij}^{2}\,.

We understand 2d log-concavity as being indicative of the sequence being log-concave “in all possible directions”. In particular if a sequence is 2d log-concave, its restriction to any row, column or diagonal in ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} is a log-concave singly-indexed sequence.

Conjecture 1.8 (2d log-concavity).

For any alternating link LL, the absolute values of the coefficients of LG⁡(L,t0,t1)\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1}) form a 2d log-concave sequence (with no interior zeros).

Definition 1.9.

We say that a two-indexed sequence (ai​j)i,j∈ℤ(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{Z}} is unimodal if, for any K≥0K\geq 0, the two-indexed sequence (ai​j​ 1|ai​j|≥K)i,j∈ℤ(a_{ij}\,\mathds{1}_{|a_{ij}|\geq K})_{i,j\in\mathbb{Z}} has no interior zeros.

Conjecture 1.10 (unimodality).

For any alternating link LL, the 2d sequence of absolute values of the coefficients of LG⁡(L,t0,t1)\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1}) is unimodal.

We will give evidence in support of these assumptions. Specifically, we show that Conjectures 1.3, 1.8, and 1.10 hold for all alternating prime knots with up to 12 crossings, as well as for several infinite families of alternating links.

Note that despite the obvious similarities between Conjectures 1.3, 1.8, and 1.10 and comparable statements for the Alexander polynomial, these conjectures are not straightforward generalizations of the well-known properties for ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t). None of the specializations from Equation (1) allow the properties of the Alexander polynomial on alternating links to be understood as consequences of the properties of the Links–Gould polynomial. This was pointed out in [Koh18] about the Ishii conjecture, and remains true here. This suggests that unlike the genus bounds and fiberedness criteria, these properties for alternating links are more likely the trace of a deep structural behavior common to both link invariants.

Let us point out that in our journey to understand whether the LG\mathrm{LG} polynomial is more closely related to the Jones polynomial or to the Alexander polynomial, these new hypothetical properties of the Links-Gould polynomial reinforce its proximity with ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t). Indeed, the Jones polynomial of an alternating link is alternating [Thi87], however, it is not always unimodal. Consider, for example,

V810​(t)=−t−6+2​t−5−4​t−4+5​t−3−4​t−2+5​t−1−3+2​t−t2.V_{8_{10}}(t)=-t^{-6}+2t^{-5}-4t^{-4}+5t^{-3}-4t^{-2}+5t^{-1}-3+2t-t^{2}.

1.4. A strengthening of the Fox-Stoimenow conjecture for the Alexander polynomial

In recent work, Hafner, Mészáros, and Vidinas proved the Fox–Stoimenow conjecture for special alternating links [HMV24] by showing that a well chosen normalization and homogenization of the Alexander polynomial is Lorentzian, a property introduced and studied by Brändén and Huh [BH20]. Observe that being Lorentzian is a very strong assumption and, as we will see, it is not satisfied by the LG\mathrm{LG} invariant for any obvious choice of variables, not even for all special alternating links. However, in the case of ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t), we show that for any alternating link, the Stoimenow extension of the Fox conjecture is equivalent to the divided power normalization of the Alexander polynomial being Lorentzian. We refer to the Definitions 3.5 and 3.8 for precise definitions of the (divided power) normalization and Lorentzian property.

Proposition 1.11 (Lorentzian property for Alexander).

The homogenized Alexander polynomial of an alternating link Homog​(ΔL​(−t))\mathrm{Homog}(\Delta_{L}(-t)) is denormalized Lorentzian if and only if the absolute values of the coefficients of the Alexander polynomial of the link form a log-concave sequence (with no internal zeros).

That the Alexander polynomial is denormalized Lorenztian follows from the structure of ΔL​(t)\Delta_{L}(t) for LL an alternating link and from Proposition 1.11, which is an application of the following elementary algebraic result.

Proposition 1.12.

For P⁡(t)P(t) a one-variable polynomial with nonnegative real coefficients, its sequence of coefficients is log-concave if and only if Q⁡(t,z):=Homog⁡(P)Q(t,z):=\mathrm{Homog}(P) is denormalized Lorentzian.

Thus, following Stoimenow [Sto05] the Alexander polynomial satisfies the Lorentzian property for all alternating knots with up to 16 crossings, and this is conjecturally true for all alternating links.

We conclude this introduction with a question.

Question 1.13.

Is the homogenized Links–Gould polynomial of alternating links denormalized Lorentzian after a proper change of variables?

1.5. Organization of the paper

Section 2 contains the definition and elementary properties of the Links–Gould link polynomial. Some basic properties of log-concave sequences are presented in Section 3, as well as the definition and characteristics of Lorentzian polynomials. In particular, log-concavity is related to unimodality and being a trapezoidal sequence. These properties will be useful to simplify the calculations carried out later in the paper. Propositions 1.11 and 1.12 are proved in Section 4 and the implications for the Fox–Stoimenow conjecture are discussed. Section 5 presents experimental and computational evidence in support of Conjectures 1.3, 1.8 and 1.10. Indeed, using a Python program [HKST] that analyzes the data from the LG\mathrm{LG}-explorer [DW], we confirm that for all alternating knots available in the LG\mathrm{LG}-explorer database, these conjectures are true. This includes all alternating knots with up to 12 crossings, and a selection of 13 to 16 crossing alternating knots with small braid index. We also show that the Links–Gould polynomial of the trefoil is not denormalized Lorenztian for various choices of variables. Moreover, we prove that all three conjectures are true for two infinite families of links: (2,n)(2,n)-torus links and twist knots. Their Links–Gould invariants are presented in the Figures of Section 6.

2. The Links-Gould polynomial: definition and properties

In this section we closely follow the ideas exposed in [GHK+c, GHK+a]. For a more representation theoretic approach to the Links–Gould invariant see [DWLK99, GHK+b].

2.1. The Reshetikhin–Turaev functor

We review briefly the well-known Reshetikhin–Turaev functor  [RT90, Tur94] from tangles to tensor products of endomorphisms of a vector space and its dual.

A tangle diagram can be decomposed into a finite number of elementary oriented tangle diagrams shown in Figure 1. Moreover, up to isotopy, we may assume that for any horizontal line drawn on the diagram there is at most one critical point or a single crossing.

Set VV a vector space over a field 𝕂\mathbbm{K} of characteristic zero and consider V∗=End⁡(V,𝕂)V^{\ast}=\mathrm{End}(V,\mathbbm{K}) its dual. Each elementary oriented tangle is associated to a linear map under the Reshetikhin-Turaev functor FF, as shown in Figure 2. By composing these elementary maps, one obtains a linear map FTF_{T} for any oriented tangle diagram TT. For example, if TT is an oriented (n,m)(n,m)-tangle diagram, then FT∈End⁡(Vϵ1⊗Vϵ2⊗…⊗Vϵn,Vδ1⊗Vδ2⊗…⊗Vδm),F_{T}\in\mathrm{End}(V^{\epsilon_{1}}\otimes V^{\epsilon_{2}}\otimes\ldots\otimes V^{\epsilon_{n}},V^{\delta_{1}}\otimes V^{\delta_{2}}\otimes\ldots\otimes V^{\delta_{m}})\,, where ϵi\epsilon_{i}, δj\delta_{j} are empty or ∗\ast, depending on the orientations of the boundary ∂T\partial T of TT.

2.2. Invariants of tangles

To state the identities of an enhanced RR-matrix we need to fix some notation. We do so following Ohtsuki [Oht02]. Fix a finite dimensional vector space VV with basis (e1,…,en)(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n}). For A∈End⁡(V⊗V)A\in\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V), we write A=(A(i,j)(k,l))A=(A_{(i,j)}^{(k,l)}) as a matrix in basis (ei⊗ej)(e_{i}\otimes e_{j}). Therefore A(i,j)(k,l)=(ek⊗el)∗​(A⁡(ei⊗ej))A_{(i,j)}^{(k,l)}=(e_{k}\otimes e_{l})^{\ast}(A(e_{i}\otimes e_{j})). Then matrices A↺A^{\circlearrowleft} and A↻A^{\circlearrowright} are defined by setting:

(A↺)(k,i)(l,j)=A(i,j)(k,l),(A↻)(j,l)(i,k)=A(i,j)(k,l).(A^{\circlearrowleft})_{(k,i)}^{(l,j)}=A_{(i,j)}^{(k,l)},\qquad(A^{\circlearrowright})_{(j,l)}^{(i,k)}=A_{(i,j)}^{(k,l)}\,.
Definition 2.1.

An enhanced RR-matrix on a finite dimensional vector space VV is a pair of invertible endomorphisms R∈End⁡(V⊗V)R\in\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V), the RR-matrix, and h∈End⁡(V)h\in\mathrm{End}(V), the enhancement, satisfying

R∘(h⊗h)\displaystyle R\circ(h\otimes h) =(h⊗h)∘R\displaystyle=(h\otimes h)\circ R (2a)
tr2​((idV⊗h)∘R±1)\displaystyle\mathrm{tr}_{2}((\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes h)\circ R^{\pm 1}) =idV\displaystyle=\mathrm{id}_{V} (2b)
(R−1)↺∘((idV⊗h)∘R∘(h−1⊗idV))↻\displaystyle(R^{-1})^{\circlearrowleft}\circ((\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes h)\circ R\circ(h^{-1}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V}))^{\circlearrowright} =idV⊗idV∗\displaystyle=\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V^{\ast}} (2c)
(R⊗idV)∘(idV⊗R)∘(R⊗idV)\displaystyle(R\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes R)\circ(R\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V}) =(idV⊗R)∘(R⊗idV)∘(idV⊗R)\displaystyle=(\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes R)\circ(R\otimes\mathrm{id}_{V})\circ(\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes R) (2d)

The partial trace tr2\mathrm{tr}_{2} of f⊗g∈End⁡(V⊗V)f\otimes g\in\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V) is defined by

tr2​(f⊗g)=tr⁡(g)​f∈End⁡(V)\mathrm{tr}_{2}(f\otimes g)=\mathrm{tr}(g)f\in\mathrm{End}(V)

with the natural identification of End⁡(V⊗V)\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V) and End⁡(V)⊗End⁡(V)\mathrm{End}(V)\otimes\mathrm{End}(V). This extends to partial trace operations tri:End⁡(V⊗n)→End⁡(V⊗n−1)\mathrm{tr}_{i}:\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n})\to\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n-1}) where we trace in the ii-th component. Let tri1i2⋯ij\mathrm{tr}_{i_{1}i_{2}\cdots i_{j}} denote the composition of partial traces tri1∘tri2∘⋯∘trij\mathrm{tr}_{i_{1}}\circ\mathrm{tr}_{i_{2}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathrm{tr}_{i_{j}}.

For 1≤i<j≤n1\leq i<j\leq n and f∈End⁡(V⊗V)f\in\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V) define (f)i​j∈End⁡(V⊗n)(f)_{ij}\in\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n}) which acts by ff in the ii-th and jj-th tensor factors and is the identity otherwise.

Given an RR-matrix, Equation (2d) defines a representation ρR\rho_{R} of the braid group BnB_{n} by mapping the elementary braid generator in position (k,k+1)(k,k+1) to (R)k,k+1∈End⁡(V⊗n)(R)_{k,k+1}\in\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n}).

Remark 2.2.

An enhanced RR-matrix determines an operator valued invariant of isotopy classes of tangles under the Reshetikhin-Turaev functor if one considers the following definitions of cup and cap maps:

2.3. Invariants of links

Assuming this, an enhanced RR-matrix on VV gives rise to an invariant FF of closed links. However, for some enhanced RR-matrices (e.g. for the LG\mathrm{LG} invariant) FF is the zero invariant. To obtain a nontrivial invariant, we consider tangles, where an enhanced RR-matrix gives an End⁡(V)\mathrm{End}(V)-valued invariant FTF_{T} of a (1,1)(1,1)-tangle TT and an End⁡(V⊗V)\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V)-valued invariant FTF_{T} of a (2,2)(2,2)-tangle with upward oriented boundary, by which we mean a tangle with two upward incoming and outgoing arcs and perhaps additional closed components. To get to a scalar-valued invariant of links, we need to ensure:

  1. (P1P_{1})

    For every (1,1)(1,1)-tangle TT, FTF_{T} is a scalar multiple of idV\mathrm{id}_{V}.

  2. (P2P_{2})

    For every (2,2)(2,2)-tangle TT defining a map FT∈End⁡(V⊗2)F_{T}\in\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes 2}) with left and right closures T1T_{1} and T2T_{2}, we have FT1=FT2∈End⁡(V)F_{T_{1}}=F_{T_{2}}\in\mathrm{End}(V).

When (( P 1 )) is satisfied and TT is a (1,1)(1,1)-tangle, we write FT=⟨FT⟩​idVF_{T}=\langle F_{T}\rangle\mathrm{id}_{V}. Properties (( P 1 )) and (( P 2 )) imply the existence of a scalar invariant of links LL obtained by cutting a link along any component to obtain a (1,1)(1,1)-tangle LcutL^{\mathrm{cut}}. We denote this modified Reshetikhin-Turaev link invariant mRTL=⟨FLcut⟩\text{mRT}_{L}=\langle F_{L^{\mathrm{cut}}}\rangle.

Remark 2.3.

When FF is determined by a ribbon category, Property (( P 1 )) is the assumption that the coloring object VV is simple. Property (( P 2 )) is the assumption that VV is an ambidextrous object in the sense of [GPMT09].

Remark 2.4.

If β∈Bn\beta\in B_{n} is a braid with closure LL, then

FLcut\displaystyle F_{L^{\mathrm{cut}}} =tr2,…,n​((idV⊗h⊗(n−1))∘ρR​(β))∈End⁡(V)\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}_{2,\dots,n}\left((\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes h^{\otimes(n-1)})\circ\rho_{R}(\beta)\right)\in\mathrm{End}(V)
⟨FLcut⟩\displaystyle\langle F_{L^{\mathrm{cut}}}\rangle =1dim(V)​tr​((idV⊗h⊗(n−1))∘ρR​(β)).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\dim(V)}\mathrm{tr}\left((\mathrm{id}_{V}\otimes h^{\otimes(n-1)})\circ\rho_{R}(\beta)\right)\,.

2.4. The LG\mathrm{LG} invariant of links

Note that in dealing with the Links–Gould invariant of links, we stick to conventions used by Ishii for example in [Ish06]. In doing so, LG⁡(L,p−2,p2​q2)\mathrm{LG}(L;p^{-2},p^{2}q^{2}) with p=qαp=q^{\alpha} coincides with the Links-Gould invariant from [DWLK99].

Suppose VV is a vector space over a field 𝕂\mathbbm{K} with an ordered basis (v1,…,vn)(v_{1},\dots,v_{n}) and an RR matrix R∈End⁡(V⊗V)R\in\mathrm{End}(V\otimes V). Abbreviating vi​j=vi⊗vjv_{ij}=v_{i}\otimes v_{j} for i,j=1,…​ni,j=1,\dots n, the n2×n2n^{2}\times n^{2} matrix RR can be presented as an n×nn\times n matrix 𝖱:=(R⁡(xi​j))1≤i,j≤n\mathsf{R}:=(R(x_{ij}))_{1\leq i,j\leq n} whose entries are 𝕂\mathbbm{K}-linear combinations of the vi​jv_{ij}.

The Links–Gould RR-matrix is defined as follows. Consider a 4-dimensional ℚ⁡(t0,t1)\mathbbm{Q}(t_{0},t_{1})-vector space WW with an ordered basis (w1,w2,w3,w4)(w_{1},w_{2},w_{3},w_{4}). Abbreviating wi​j=wi⊗wjw_{ij}=w_{i}\otimes w_{j} for i,j=1,…​4i,j=1,\dots 4, the RR-matrix 𝖱LG:=((RLG)​(wi​j))1≤i,j≤4\mathsf{R}_{\mathrm{LG}}:=((R_{\mathrm{LG}})(w_{ij}))_{1\leq i,j\leq 4} is given by

𝖱LG=(t0​w11t01/2​w21t01/2​w31w41t01/2​w12+(t0−1)​w21−w22(t0​t1−1)​w23−t01/2​t11/2​w32−t01/2​t11/2​Y​w41t11/2​w42t01/2​w13+(t0−1)​w31−t01/2​t11/2​w23+Y​w41−w33t11/2​w43w14−t01/2​t11/2​Y​w23+Y​w32+Y2​w41t11/2​w24+(t1−1)​w42t11/2​w34+(t1−1)​w43t1​w44)\mathsf{R}_{\mathrm{LG}}=\left(\begin{array}[]{@{}cccc}t_{0}w_{11}&t_{0}^{1/2}w_{21}&t_{0}^{1/2}w_{31}&w_{41}\\ t_{0}^{1/2}w_{12}+(t_{0}-1)w_{21}&-w_{22}&(t_{0}t_{1}-1)w_{23}-t_{0}^{1/2}t_{1}^{1/2}w_{32}-t_{0}^{1/2}t_{1}^{1/2}Yw_{41}&t_{1}^{1/2}w_{42}\\ t_{0}^{1/2}w_{13}+(t_{0}-1)w_{31}&-t_{0}^{1/2}t_{1}^{1/2}w_{23}+Yw_{41}&-w_{33}&t_{1}^{1/2}w_{43}\\ w_{14}-t_{0}^{1/2}t_{1}^{1/2}Yw_{23}+Yw_{32}+Y^{2}w_{41}&t_{1}^{1/2}w_{24}+(t_{1}-1)w_{42}&t_{1}^{1/2}w_{34}+(t_{1}-1)w_{43}&t_{1}w_{44}\end{array}\right)

with Y=(t0−1)​(1−t1)Y=\sqrt{(t_{0}-1)(1-t_{1})}.

Remark 2.5.

The entries in the above matrix are in the quadratic extension ℚ⁡(t0,t1)​[Y]\mathbbm{Q}(t_{0},t_{1})[Y] of the field ℚ⁡(t0,t1)\mathbbm{Q}(t_{0},t_{1}).

Define also hLG=diag⁡(t0−1,−t1,−t0−1,t1)∈End⁡(W)h_{\mathrm{LG}}=\mathrm{diag}(t_{0}^{-1},-t_{1},-t_{0}^{-1},t_{1})\in\mathrm{End}(W).

Lemma 2.6.

(RLG,hLG)(R_{\mathrm{LG}},h_{\mathrm{LG}}) is an enhanced RR-matrix and satisfies properties (( P 1 )) and (( P 2 )).

Definition 2.7.

The Links–Gould polynomial invariant of a link LL is defined from the previous enhanced RR-matrix by setting LG⁡(L,t0,t1)=⟨FLcut⟩.\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1})=\langle F_{L^{\mathrm{cut}}}\rangle.

Remark 2.8.

Though it is not obvious at first glance, one can show that LG⁡(L,t0,t1)∈ℤ⁡[t0±1,t1±1]\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1})\in\mathbb{Z}[t_{0}^{\pm 1},t_{1}^{\pm 1}], see [Ish06, Theorem 1] and [GHK+a, Theorem 1].

The elementary properties of LG\mathrm{LG} mirror features of the Alexander-Conway polynomial, some of which are listed below.

Proposition 2.9.

The Links-Gould polynomial satisfies the following properties.

  1. (1)

    LG⁡(○)=1\mathrm{LG}(\bigcirc)=1 .

  2. (2)

    Denoting L∗L^{*} the reflection of LL, we have

    LG⁡(L∗,t0,t1)=LG⁡(L,t0−1,t1−1).\mathrm{LG}(L^{*};t_{0},t_{1})=\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0}^{-1},t_{1}^{-1})\,.
  3. (3)

    The symmetry

    LG⁡(L,t0,t1)=LG⁡(L,t1,t0)\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{0},t_{1})=\mathrm{LG}(L;t_{1},t_{0})

    holds. When taken together with the fact that link inversion switches the variables t0t_{0} and t1t_{1}, it implies that LG\mathrm{LG} does not detect inversion.

  4. (4)

    For two links LL and L′L^{\prime}, denoting their connected sum by L​#​L′L\#L^{\prime}, we have

    LG⁡(L​#​L′)=LG⁡(L)​LG​(L′).\mathrm{LG}(L\#L^{\prime})=\mathrm{LG}(L)\,\mathrm{LG}(L^{\prime})\,.
  5. (5)

    If L=L′⊔L′′L=L^{\prime}\sqcup L^{\prime\prime} is the split union of links L′L^{\prime} and L′′L^{\prime\prime}, then

    LG⁡(L)=0.\mathrm{LG}(L)=0\,.

A (rather complicated) complete set of skein relations for LG\mathrm{LG} was recently presented in [GHK+a].

3. Log-concavity, unimodality, Lorentzian polynomials: properties, examples, counter-examples

3.1. Log-concavity, unimodality

First we give some elementary properties of log-concave sequences that will be helpful in the next section. The following definitions, as mentioned in the introduction, are recalled below.

We say that a sequence (ai)i∈ℤ(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is log-concave if, for every i∈ℤi\in\mathbb{Z}, we have:

ai−1​ai+1≤ai2.a_{i-1}\,a_{i+1}\leq a_{i}^{2}\,.

Likewise, we refer to a bidimensional sequence (ai​j)i,j∈ℤ(a_{ij})_{i,j\in\mathbb{Z}} as 2d log-concave if for every i,j,k,l∈ℤi,j,k,l\in\mathbb{Z} :

ai+k,j+l​ai−k,j−l≤ai​j2.a_{i+k,j+l}\,a_{i-k,j-l}\leq a_{ij}^{2}\,.
Proposition 3.1.

For (ai)i∈ℤ(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} a log-concave sequence of non-negative real numbers with no internal zeros, the sequence (ai/ai−1)i∈ℤ(a_{i}/a_{i-1})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is non-increasing.

Corollary 3.2.

If (ai)i∈ℤ(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is a log-concave sequence of non-negative real numbers with no internal zeros, then the sequence is trapezoidal and, in particular, it is unimodal.

Proof.

The sequence (ri)=(ai/ai−1)(r_{i})=(a_{i}/a_{i-1}) is non-increasing on the interval where it is well-defined. So for some −∞≤p≤q≤+∞-\infty\leq p\leq q\leq+\infty one can write:

ri>1⇔i≤p, and ri<1⇔i≥q.r_{i}>1\iff i\leq p\,,\qquad\text{ and }\qquad r_{i}<1\iff i\geq q\,.

This precisely means that (ai)(a_{i}) is trapezoidal and therefore unimodal. ∎

Remark 3.3.

Corollary 3.2 is not true if one does not assume that the sequence does not have internal zeros. Indeed, a sequence can have multiple local maxima and still be log-concave, as long as the “bumps” are far apart enough. Consider for example:

(ai)=(…,0,1,0,0,1,0,0,…).(a_{i})=(\ldots,0,1,0,0,1,0,0,\ldots)\,.
Corollary 3.4.

[Generalized log-concavity inequality] Suppose (ai)i∈ℤ(a_{i})_{i\in\mathbb{Z}} is a log-concave sequence of non-negative real numbers with no internal zeros. For all i,k∈ℤi,k\in\mathbb{Z}, we have:

ai−k​ai+k≤ai2.a_{i-k}\,a_{i+k}\leq a_{i}^{2}\,.
Proof.

If any of the three terms is zero, then the inequality obviously holds, because the sequence has no internal zeros. So we can suppose that all three terms are nonzero. In that case, the inequality we wish to prove can be written as follows:

ai+kai≤aiai−k.\frac{a_{i+k}}{a_{i}}\,\leq\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-k}}\,.

But we know that the sequence (ai/ai−1)(a_{i}/a_{i-1}) is non-increasing and thus:

bi=aiai−k=aiai−1×ai−1ai−2×…×ai−k+1ai−kb_{i}=\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-k}}=\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-1}}\times\frac{a_{i-1}}{a_{i-2}}\times\ldots\times\frac{a_{i-k+1}}{a_{i-k}}

is the product of kk positive non-increasing sequences. So (bi)(b_{i}) is a non-increasing sequence and we have:

bi+k≤bi, i.e. ai+kai≤aiai−k.∎b_{i+k}\leq b_{i}\,,\quad\text{ i.e. }\quad\frac{a_{i+k}}{a_{i}}\,\leq\frac{a_{i}}{a_{i-k}}\,.\qed

3.2. Lorentzian polynomials

We define the d-th discrete simplex Δmd⊆ℕm\Delta_{m}^{d}\subseteq\mathbb{N}^{m} by

Δmd={α∈ℕm|∑iαi=d}.\Delta_{m}^{d}=\{{\alpha\in\mathbb{N}^{m}~|~\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}=d\,\}}\,.

For any 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, we denote by ϵi\epsilon_{i} the unit vector in the i-th coordinate.

The notation wαw^{\alpha} stands for ∏i=1mwiαi\prod\limits_{i=1}^{m}w_{i}^{\alpha_{i}} and ∂α=∂1α1⋯∂mαm\partial^{\alpha}=\partial_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots\partial_{m}^{\alpha_{m}}. We also introduce α!=∏i=1mαi!\alpha!=\prod\limits_{i=1}^{m}\alpha_{i}!.

Definition 3.5.

An mm-variable homogeneous polynomial PP of degree dd with nonnegative real coefficients is strictly Lorentzian if for any α∈Δmd−2\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d-2}, ∂αP\partial^{\alpha}P is a nondegenerate quadratic form of signature (1,m−1)(1,m-1).

Definition 3.6.

A subset Σ\Sigma of ℕm\mathbb{N}^{m} is M\mathrm{M}-convex if for any index ii and any α,β∈Σ\alpha,\beta\in\Sigma whose ii-th coordinates satisfy αi>βi\alpha_{i}>\beta_{i}, there exists an index jj such that

αj<βj,α−ϵi+ϵj∈Σ,β−ϵj+ϵi∈Σ.\alpha_{j}<\beta_{j}\,,\quad\alpha-\epsilon_{i}+\epsilon_{j}\in\Sigma\,,\quad\beta-\epsilon_{j}+\epsilon_{i}\in\Sigma\,.

The set of degree dd homogeneous polynomials in mm variables with nonnegative coefficients and an M\mathrm{M}-convex support is denoted by Mmd\mathrm{M}_{m}^{d}.

Definition 3.7.

A homogeneous real polynomial is Lorentzian if it is the limit of strictly Lorentzian polynomials of the same degree and in the same number of variables.

Brändén and Huh [BH20] prove that in the space of degree dd homogeneous polynomials in mm variables with real coefficients, the set of Lorentzian polynomials Lmd\mathrm{L}_{m}^{d} can be described completely: Lm2\mathrm{L}_{m}^{2} is the set of degree 22 homogeneous polynomials with nonnegative coefficients and at most one positive eigenvalue. For d>2d>2, we have

Lmd={P∈Mmd:∂αP∈Lm2​ for any α∈Δmd−2}.\mathrm{L}_{m}^{d}=\{P\in\mathrm{M}_{m}^{d}:\partial^{\alpha}P\in\mathrm{L}_{m}^{2}\text{ for any $\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d-2}$}\}\,.
Definition 3.8.

Given a homogeneous polynomial of degree dd in mm variables P=∑α∈Δmdcα​wαP=\sum\limits_{\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d}}c_{\alpha}w^{\alpha}, we define its normalization 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) by setting

𝒩⁡(P)=∑α∈Δmdcα​wαα!.\mathcal{N}(P)=\sum\limits_{\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d}}\frac{c_{\alpha}w^{\alpha}}{\alpha!}\,.

As shown in Proposition 4.4 of [BH20], we have the following.

Proposition 3.9.

Given a homogeneous polynomial P=∑α∈Δmdcα​wαP=\sum\limits_{\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d}}c_{\alpha}w^{\alpha}, if 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) is Lorentzian, then the coefficients of PP satisfy cα+ϵi−ϵj​cα−ϵi+ϵj≤cα2c_{\alpha+\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}}c_{\alpha-\epsilon_{i}+\epsilon_{j}}\leq c_{\alpha}^{2}.

Let us state a few stability properties satisfied by Lorentzian polynomials.

Proposition 3.10 ([BH20, Corollary 3.8]).

Given two homogeneous polynomials PP and QQ, if 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) and 𝒩⁡(Q)\mathcal{N}(Q) are Lorentzian, then 𝒩⁡(P​Q)\mathcal{N}(PQ) is also Lorentzian.

Note that the converse does not hold. For example, let f=6​x3+2​x​y2+6​a​y3f=6x^{3}+2xy^{2}+6ay^{3} with 𝒩⁡(f)=x3+x​y2+a​y3\mathcal{N}(f)=x^{3}+xy^{2}+ay^{3}. Then 𝒩⁡(f2)\mathcal{N}(f^{2}) is Lorentzian, but for a∈(−618,0)a\in(-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{18},0), 𝒩⁡(f)\mathcal{N}(f) is not Lorentzian.

Proposition 3.11.

If P⁡(w1,…,wm)P(w_{1},\dots,w_{m}) is a homogeneous polynomial and wk−1​P​(w1,…,wm)w_{k}^{-1}P(w_{1},\dots,w_{m}) is also a polynomial, then 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) is Lorentzian if and only if 𝒩⁡(wk−1​P)\mathcal{N}(w_{k}^{-1}P) is Lorentzian.

Proof.

The reverse implication follows from Proposition 3.10. To prove the forward implication, assume 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) is Lorentzian and write P=∑α∈Δmdcα​wαP=\sum\limits_{\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d}}c_{\alpha}w^{\alpha}. Then

𝒩⁡(wk−1​P)=∑α∈Δmdcα​wα−ϵk(α−ϵk)!.\mathcal{N}(w_{k}^{-1}P)=\sum\limits_{\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d}}\frac{c_{\alpha}w^{\alpha-\epsilon_{k}}}{(\alpha-\epsilon_{k})!}\,.

By assumption cα=0c_{\alpha}=0 whenever αk=0\alpha_{k}=0, thus the above sum is well-defined. Equivalently, we assume that α≥ek\alpha\geq e_{k}. Note that 𝒩⁡(wk−1​P)\mathcal{N}(w_{k}^{-1}P) is of degree d−1d-1. Fix γ∈Δmd−3\gamma\in\Delta_{m}^{d-3}. Then

∂γ[𝒩⁡(wk−1​P)]=∑α∈Δmdα≥γ+ϵkcα​wα−ϵk−γ(α−ϵk−γ)!=∑β∈Δm2cγ+ϵk+β​wββ!{\partial^{\gamma}}[\mathcal{N}(w_{k}^{-1}P)]=\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}\alpha\in\Delta_{m}^{d}\\ \alpha\geq\gamma+\epsilon_{k}\end{subarray}}\frac{c_{\alpha}w^{\alpha-\epsilon_{k}-\gamma}}{(\alpha-\epsilon_{k}-\gamma)!}=\sum\limits_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\in\Delta_{m}^{2}\end{subarray}}\frac{c_{\gamma+\epsilon_{k}+\beta}w^{\beta}}{\beta!}

is a degree two polynomial. The matrix entries of the Hessian H~γ\tilde{H}^{\gamma} of ∂γ[𝒩⁡(P)]{\partial^{\gamma}}[\mathcal{N}(P)] are (H~γ)i​j=cγ+ϵk+ϵi+ϵj(\tilde{H}^{\gamma})_{ij}=c_{\gamma+\epsilon_{k}+\epsilon_{i}+\epsilon_{j}}.

A similar computation shows that the Hessian Hγ+ϵkH^{\gamma+\epsilon_{k}} of ∂γ+ϵk[𝒩⁡(P)]\partial^{\gamma+\epsilon_{k}}[\mathcal{N}(P)] satisfies Hγ+ϵk=H~γH^{\gamma+\epsilon_{k}}=\tilde{H}^{\gamma}. Since Hγ+ϵkH^{\gamma+\epsilon_{k}} has at most one positive eigenvalue, so does H~γ\tilde{H}^{\gamma} and 𝒩⁡(wk−1​P)\mathcal{N}(w_{k}^{-1}P) is Lorenztian. ∎

In addition, the next result has been proved as Lemma 4.8 in [BLP23].

Proposition 3.12.

Set P⁡(w1,…,wm)P(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m}) a homogeneous polynomial and Q⁡(w1,…,wm−1):=P⁡(w1,…,wm−1,wm−1)Q(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m-1}):=P(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m-1},w_{m-1}). If 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) is Lorentzian, then so is 𝒩⁡(Q)\mathcal{N}(Q).

4. Proof of Propositions 1.11 and 1.12

We recall some ideas developed by Crowell [Cro59]. Fix an alternating link LL with alternating diagram DD. Because DD is alternating, coloring S2S^{2} following the rule shown in Figure 4 produces a coherent checkerboard coloring of the plane.

Moreover, if one applies the transformation shown in Figure 5, one defines an orientation oo on the four-valent graph underlying DD which differs from the orientation inherited from LL. Denote this oriented graph by PP and let ww denote the map which assigns a weight to each edge of PP, still following Figure 5.

For any vertex ii of PP, we define Tree⁡(i)\mathrm{Tree}(i) to be the set of all rooted trees of PP with respect to the orientation oo and with origin ii containing all the vertices of PP. Note that a rooted tree is a subgraph that forms a tree and no two edges share the same terminal vertex.

Theorem 4.1 ([Cro59]).

For any ii vertex of PP, the Alexander polynomial of an alternating link LL can be expressed as follows:

ΔL​(t)=∑T∈Tree⁡(i)(∏e​edge​of​Tw⁡(e)).\Delta_{L}(t)=\sum\limits_{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i)}\left(\prod\limits_{e\,\mathrm{edge}\,\mathrm{of}\,T}w(e)\right).

For TT a rooted tree, one can define c​h​a​r​(T)char(T) as the number of edges ee of TT that have weight w⁡(e)=−tw(e)=-t. In other words,

c​h​a​r​(T)=#⁡(w−1​(−t)∩T).char(T)=\#(w^{-1}(-t)\cap T)\,.
Proposition 4.2 ([Cro59]).

For LL an alternating link, if ΔL​(t)=∑k=pqak​tk\Delta_{L}(t)=\sum\limits_{k=p}^{q}a_{k}\,t^{k} with ap,aq≠0a_{p},a_{q}\neq 0, then q−p=v−f+1q-p=v-f+1, where vv is the number of vertices and ff is the number of Seifert circles of DD.

Proposition 4.3.

Up to an invertible element of ℤ⁡[t±1]\mathbb{Z}[t^{\pm 1}], we have for any alternating link LL:

ΔL​(t)​=˙​∑k=0v−f+1#⁡{T∈Tree⁡(i):c​h​a​r​(T)=k}​(−t)k.\Delta_{L}(t)\,\dot{=}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{v-f+1}\#\{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i):char(T)=k\}\,(-t)^{k}.
Proof.

The proposition is a consequence of the following computation:

ΔL​(t)\displaystyle\Delta_{L}(t) =∑T∈Tree⁡(i)(∏e​edge​of​Tw⁡(e))\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i)}\left(\prod\limits_{e\,\mathrm{edge}\,\mathrm{of}\,T}w(e)\right)
=∑k=pq#⁡{T∈Tree⁡(i):c​h​a​r​(T)=k}​(−t)k\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{k=p}^{q}\#\{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i):char(T)=k\}\,(-t)^{k}
=˙​∑k=0q−p#⁡{T∈Tree⁡(i):c​h​a​r​(T)=k}​(−t)k\displaystyle\,\,\dot{=}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{q-p}\#\{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i):char(T)=k\}\,(-t)^{k}
=∑k=0v−f+1#⁡{T∈Tree⁡(i):c​h​a​r​(T)=k}​(−t)k​ (see Proposition 4.2).∎\displaystyle\,\,{=}\sum\limits_{k=0}^{v-f+1}\#\{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i):char(T)=k\}\,(-t)^{k}\text{ (see Proposition~\ref{maxdeg})}\,.\qed

In addition, Crowell proves in [Cro59] that for 0≤k≤v−f+10\leq k\leq v-f+1, the set {T∈Tree⁡(i):c​h​a​r​(T)=k}\{T\in\mathrm{Tree}(i):char(T)=k\} is non empty. Therefore, the latter proves Proposition 1.11 modulo Proposition 1.12, and we now wish to prove Proposition 1.12. Before that we recall some definitions.

Definition 4.4.

Let PP be an mm-variable polynomial of degree dd

P⁡(w1,…,wm−1,wm)=∑i1,i2,…,imci1,i2,…,im​∏k=1mwikαik.P(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m-1},w_{m})=\sum\limits_{i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{m}}c_{i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{m}}\prod\limits_{k=1}^{m}w_{i_{k}}^{\alpha_{i_{k}}}\,.

The homogenization of PP is the homogeneous polynomial of degree dd

Homog⁡(P)​(w1,…,wm−1,wm,z)=∑i1,i2,…,imci1,i2,…,im​(∏k=1mwikαik)​zd−αi1−…−αim.\mathrm{Homog}(P)(w_{1},\ldots,w_{m-1},w_{m},z)=\sum\limits_{i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{m}}c_{i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{m}}\left(\prod\limits_{k=1}^{m}w_{i_{k}}^{\alpha_{i_{k}}}\right)z^{d-\alpha_{i_{1}}-\ldots-\alpha_{i_{m}}}.
Definition 4.5.

A homogeneous polynomial PP is called denormalized Lorentzian if 𝒩⁡(P)\mathcal{N}(P) is Lorentzian.

Proof of Proposition 1.12.

We write

P⁡(t)=∑k=0dck​tk,xk≥0,xd≠0.P(t)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{d}c_{k}\,t^{k}\,,\quad x_{k}\geq 0\,,\quad x_{d}\neq 0\,.

To translate the Lorentzian condition in terms of coefficients of the polynomial, we can now compute the partial derivatives of

Q⁡(t,z)=𝒩∘Homog⁡(P)=∑k=0dck​tk​zd−kk!​(d−k)!.Q(t,z)=\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(P)=\sum\limits_{k=0}^{d}\frac{c_{k}\,t^{k}z^{d-k}}{k!(d-k)!}\,.

Set a,b∈ℤa,b\in\mathbb{Z} such that 0≤a≤d−20\leq a\leq d-2 and a+b=d−2a+b=d-2. Then

∂aQ∂ta​(t,z)\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{a}Q}{\partial t^{a}}(t,z) =∑k=adck(k−a)!​(d−k)!​tk−a​zd−k\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{k=a}^{d}\frac{c_{k}}{(k-a)!(d-k)!}\,t^{k-a}z^{d-k}

and

∂a+bQ∂zb​∂ta​(t,z)\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{a+b}Q}{\partial z^{b}\partial t^{a}}(t,z) =∑k=aa+2ck(k−a)!​(a+2−k)!​tk−a​za+2−k=ca2​z2+ca+1​t​z+ca+22​t2.\displaystyle=\sum\limits_{k=a}^{a+2}\frac{c_{k}}{(k-a)!(a+2-k)!}\,t^{k-a}z^{a+2-k}=\frac{c_{a}}{2}z^{2}+c_{a+1}tz+\frac{c_{a+2}}{2}t^{2}\,.

The Hessian matrix for ∂a+bQ∂zb​∂ta​(t,z)\frac{\partial^{a+b}Q}{\partial z^{b}\partial t^{a}}(t,z) relative to the derivatives ∂z,∂t\partial z,\partial t is:

(caca+1ca+1ca+2)\begin{pmatrix}c_{a}&c_{a+1}\\ c_{a+1}&c_{a+2}\end{pmatrix}

with characteristic polynomial and discriminant

χa​(λ)=λ2−(ca+ca+2)​λ+ca​ca+2−ca+12andΔa=(ca−ca+2)2+4​ca+12≥0.\displaystyle\chi_{a}(\lambda)=\lambda^{2}-(c_{a}+c_{a+2})\lambda+c_{a}c_{a+2}-c_{a+1}^{2}\qquad\mbox{and}\qquad\Delta_{a}=(c_{a}-c_{a+2})^{2}+4c_{a+1}^{2}\geq 0\,.

The Lorentzian property for Q⁡(t,z)Q(t,z) means that the smaller root of χa\chi_{a} is nonpositive. In other words, ca+ca+2−Δa≤0c_{a}+c_{a+2}-\sqrt{\Delta_{a}}\leq 0 for any 0≤a≤d−20\leq a\leq d-2. Since all the cic_{i} are nonnegative, this last inequality is equivalent to ca​ca+2≤ca+12c_{a}c_{a+2}\leq c_{a+1}^{2}, which exactly means that the sequence (ci)(c_{i}) of coefficients of PP is log-concave. This proves Proposition 1.12. ∎

Proposition 1.11 shines a new light on the Fox-Stoimenow conjecture. Indeed, it suggests that a reasonable strategy to attempt to prove this conjecture in full generality is to further pursue the Hafner–Mészáros–Vidinas approach [HMV24]. From Proposition 3.11, the Lorentzian property of the denormalized Alexander polynomial is independent of its presentation as an honest polynomial.

Moreover, assuming that the Fox–Stoimenow conjecture is true, Proposition 3.10 implies that the homogenization of the square of the Alexander polynomial Homog⁡(ΔL​(−t)2)\mathrm{Homog}(\Delta_{L}(-t)^{2}) for an alternating link LL is also denormalized Lorentzian, and in turn its sequence of coefficients is log-concave, see Proposition 3.9. Recall that the square of the Alexander polynomial is a specialization of the Links–Gould invariant of links, see Equation (1). This observation suggests that some form of the Fox–Stoimenow conjecture lifts to LG\mathrm{LG}, which we formulate in Conjectures 1.3, 1.8, and 1.10.

Regarding the Lorentzian property for LG\mathrm{LG}, note that it is sensitive to the choice of variables used to write the polynomial. Although the tests we carried out have failed for the obvious choices of variables, see Subsection 5.4, it is our prediction that LG\mathrm{LG} is Lorentzian for some choice of variables yet to be determined. Indeed, the 2d log-concavity property that was tested successfully shows that LG\mathrm{LG} displays a very structured behavior on alternating links.

5. Evidence supporting Conjectures 1.3, 1.8 and 1.10

5.1. The conjectures hold for all knots from the LG-explorer

We wrote a Python program that analyzes the data from De Wit’s LG\mathrm{LG}-explorer [DW] to show that conjectures 1.3, 1.8 and 1.10 are true for all prime knots with up to 12 crossings and a selection of prime knots with 13 to 16 crossings and a small braid index, for which the value of the Links-Gould polynomial is available in the LG\mathrm{LG}-explorer database. The results of the computations and verifications as well as the computer program are available online [HKST]. See Figure 6 for an example of a graphical representation of the data.

Note that there is an inconsistency in the LG\mathrm{LG}-explorer database between knots with at most 12 crossings and those with more than 12 crossings. Indeed, once you make the usual substitution

(t0,t1)=(q−2​α,q2​α+2)(t_{0},t_{1})=(q^{-2\alpha},q^{2\alpha+2})

the polynomials from the dataset are LG⁡(K,t0,t1)\mathrm{LG}(K;t_{0},t_{1}) when KK has at least 13 crossings, but for knots with 12 crossings or less the knot polynomials are LG⁡(K,t0−1,t1−1)\mathrm{LG}(K;t_{0}^{-1},t_{1}^{-1}).

5.2. The conjectures hold for all (2,n)(2,n)-torus links

Setting n∈ℤn≥1n\in\mathbb{Z}_{n\geq 1}, the (2,n)(2,n)-torus link T⁡(2,n)T(2,n) is the closure of the braid bn=σ1n∈B2b_{n}=\sigma_{1}^{n}\in B_{2}. The (2,3)(2,3)-torus link T⁡(2,3)T(2,3) is represented in Figure 7. When nn is odd, T⁡(2,n)T(2,n) is a knot; when nn is even, T⁡(2,n)T(2,n) is a link with two components. In both cases, T⁡(2,n)T(2,n) is alternating.

Lemma 5.1.

For n∈ℤn≥1n\in\mathbb{Z}_{n\geq 1}:

LG⁡(T⁡(2,n))=(−1)n−1+∑k=2n(t1n−k​t0​∑l=0k−2t0l​(−1)k−2−l−t1n−k+1​∑m=0k−1t0m​(−1)k−1−m)\mathrm{LG}(T(2,n))={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(-1)^{n-1}}+\sum\limits_{k=2}^{n}\left({\color[rgb]{0,0.7,0.3}t_{1}^{n-k}t_{0}\sum\limits_{l=0}^{k-2}t_{0}^{l}(-1)^{k-2-l}}-{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}t_{1}^{n-k+1}\sum\limits_{m=0}^{k-1}t_{0}^{m}(-1)^{k-1-m}}\right)
Proof.

Applying the partial trace to these tangles to evaluate LG\mathrm{LG} gives

L​G​(T⁡(2,n))=\displaystyle LG(T(2,n))= ((−1)n(t0+1)​(t1+1)+t0n(t0+1)​(t0−t1)+t1n(t1+1)​(t1−t0))⋅(t0+t1−t0​t1−1)\displaystyle\left(\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(t_{0}+1)(t_{1}+1)}+\frac{t_{0}^{n}}{(t_{0}+1)(t_{0}-t_{1})}+\frac{t_{1}^{n}}{(t_{1}+1)(t_{1}-t_{0})}\right)\cdot(t_{0}+t_{1}-t_{0}t_{1}-1)
−((−1)n​(t0+t1)(t0+1)​(t1+1)+t0n​(t1−1)(t0+1)​(t0−t1)+t1n​(t0−1)(t1+1)​(t1−t0))\displaystyle-\left(\frac{(-1)^{n}(t_{0}+t_{1})}{(t_{0}+1)(t_{1}+1)}+\frac{t_{0}^{n}(t_{1}-1)}{(t_{0}+1)(t_{0}-t_{1})}+\frac{t_{1}^{n}(t_{0}-1)}{(t_{1}+1)(t_{1}-t_{0})}\right)

where (t0+t1−t0​t1−1)(t_{0}+t_{1}-t_{0}t_{1}-1) is the value on the Hopf link and the trace of the identity resolution vanishes. Then we reduce the expression in order to clear the denominators. We rearrange the terms and with some patience we get the expected formula. ∎

Proposition 5.2.

Conjectures 1.3, 1.8, and 1.10 hold for all (2,n)(2,n)-torus links.

Proof.

From the expression for LG⁡(T⁡(2,n))\mathrm{LG}(T(2,n)) given in Lemma 5.1, it follows at once that Conjecture 1.3 is satisfied. Expanding on that, we draw the graph representing the absolute value of the coefficient in front of the monomial t0i​t1jt_{0}^{i}t_{1}^{j} as a function of (i,j)(i,j), see Figure 10. The graph is obtained by adding the different “layers” of coefficients in the formula from Lemma 5.1: the green layer, the blue layer, and the isolated red coefficient. Figure 10 shows clearly that Conjecture 1.10 is true.

To prove Conjecture 1.8, we want to show that the mountain of absolute values |ai,j||a_{i,j}| of coefficients of LG⁡(T⁡(2,n))\mathrm{LG}(T(2,n)) is 2d log-concave. The only possible values for |ai,j||a_{i,j}| are in the set {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}. If a,b,c∈{0,1,2}a,b,c\in\{0,1,2\} with c≠0c\neq 0, which we can suppose since (ai,j)(a_{i,j}) has no interior zeros, are three coefficients of LG⁡(T⁡(2,n))\mathrm{LG}(T(2,n)), let us see that a​b≤c2ab\leq c^{2}.
∙\bullet

(a,b,c)=(0,0,0)(a,b,c)=(0,0,0) : 0×0≤02=00\times 0\leq 0^{2}=0;
∙\bullet

(a,b,c)=(0,0,1)(a,b,c)=(0,0,1) : 0×0≤12=10\times 0\leq 1^{2}=1;
∙\bullet

(a,b,c)=(0,0,2)(a,b,c)=(0,0,2) : 0×0≤22=40\times 0\leq 2^{2}=4;
In fact, if aa or bb is zero, the computation is similar to one of the previous cases. So the remaining cases to study are when a≠0a\neq 0 and b≠0b\neq 0.
∙\bullet

(a,b)=(1,1)(a,b)=(1,1) : Then c=1c=1 or c=2c=2 because of Figure 10, and the inequality holds;
∙\bullet

(a,b)=(1,2)(a,b)=(1,2) or (2,1)(2,1) : then c=2c=2 like in the previous case, and the inequality is satisfied;
∙\bullet

(a,b)=(2,2)(a,b)=(2,2) : once again c=2c=2 because of Figure 10. So the inequality is also verified in this last case.

This concludes the proof of Conjecture 1.8 for (2,n)(2,n)-torus links. ∎

5.3. The conjectures hold for all twist knots

A twist knot is a Whitehead double of the unknot. We will denote by KnK_{n} the twist knot shown in Figure 8 when 2​n−12n-1 is positive. If 2​n−12n-1 is negative, there are 1−2​n1-2n crossings of the opposite sort.

Lemma 5.3.

For n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z}, the value of the Links–Gould polynomial on the twist knot KnK_{n} is as follows:
∙\bullet for n=0n=0: LG⁡(K0)=LG⁡(○)=1;\mathrm{LG}(K_{0})=\mathrm{LG}(\bigcirc)=1;
∙\bullet for n≤−1n\leq-1, setting l=−nl=-n :

LG⁡(Kn)\displaystyle\mathrm{LG}(K_{n}) =1+(2−t0−t1−t0−1−t1−1+t0​t1+t0−1​t1−1)​∑k=0l−1(t0​t1)k\displaystyle={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}1}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.7,0.3}(2-t_{0}-t_{1}-t_{0}^{-1}-t_{1}^{-1}+t_{0}t_{1}+t_{0}^{-1}t_{1}^{-1})\sum\limits_{k=0}^{l-1}(t_{0}t_{1})^{k}}
+(4−2t0−2t1−2t0−1−2t1−1+t0t1+t0−1t1−1+t0t1−1+t0−1t1)∑k=0l−1(2l−2k−1)(t0t1)k;\displaystyle+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(4-2t_{0}-2t_{1}-2t_{0}^{-1}-2t_{1}^{-1}+t_{0}t_{1}+t_{0}^{-1}t_{1}^{-1}+t_{0}t_{1}^{-1}+t_{0}^{-1}t_{1})\sum\limits_{k=0}^{l-1}(2l-2k-1)(t_{0}t_{1})^{k}}\,;

∙\bullet for n≥1n\geq 1, writing the formula in terms of the variables (t0−1,t1−1)(t_{0}^{-1},t_{1}^{-1}) for clarity:

LG⁡(Kn)​(t0−1,t1−1)\displaystyle\mathrm{LG}(K_{n})(t_{0}^{-1},t_{1}^{-1}) =(t0​t1)n−1​(−t02​t1−t0​t12+t02+t12+2​t0​t1−t0−t1+1)\displaystyle={\color[rgb]{1,0,0}(t_{0}t_{1})^{n-1}(-t_{0}^{2}t_{1}-t_{0}t_{1}^{2}+t_{0}^{2}+t_{1}^{2}+2t_{0}t_{1}-t_{0}-t_{1}+1)}
+(t02t12−3t02t1−3t0t12+2t02+2t12+5t0t1−3t0−3t1+2)∑k=0n−2(t0t1)k\displaystyle+{\color[rgb]{0,0.7,0.3}(t_{0}^{2}t_{1}^{2}-3t_{0}^{2}t_{1}-3t_{0}t_{1}^{2}+2t_{0}^{2}+2t_{1}^{2}+5t_{0}t_{1}-3t_{0}-3t_{1}+2)\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-2}(t_{0}t_{1})^{k}}
+(t02t12−2t02t1−2t0t12+t02+t12+4t0t1−2t0−2t1+1)∑k=0n−2(2n−2k−3)(t0t1)k.\displaystyle+{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(t_{0}^{2}t_{1}^{2}-2t_{0}^{2}t_{1}-2t_{0}t_{1}^{2}+t_{0}^{2}+t_{1}^{2}+4t_{0}t_{1}-2t_{0}-2t_{1}+1)\sum\limits_{k=0}^{n-2}(2n-2k-3)(t_{0}t_{1})^{k}}.
Proof.

We apply [Koh18, Prop. 2.18] to expand and simplify the given expressions. ∎

By adding the three layers of each formula, shown in different colors, we obtain the graphs in Figures 11 and 12.

Proposition 5.4.

Conjectures 1.3, 1.8, and 1.10 hold for all twist knots.

Proof.

Conjectures 1.3 and 1.10 are straightforward consequences of the formulas from Lemma 5.3 and carefully observing Figures 11 and 12. The proof of Conjecture 1.8 is far more tedious. Let us prove that LG⁡(Kn)\mathrm{LG}(K_{n}) satisfies the conjecture for n≤−1n\leq-1 by induction on l=−nl=-n. The other case works the same way.

The knot Kn=K−lK_{n}=K_{-l} has 2+(1+2​l)=2​l+32+(1+2l)=2l+3 crossings. So for l≤4l\leq 4, we know that 1.8 is verified for K−lK_{-l} because of prior verifications for knots with up to 1212 crossings. Suppose that for some l≥1l\geq 1, K−lK_{-l} satisfies Conjecture 1.8. We show that K−l−1K_{-l-1} also satisfies 1.8. Indeed, using Figure 11, the lower-left corner of the table of coefficients for LG⁡(K−l−1)\mathrm{LG}(K_{-l-1}) is given in Figure 9.

Outside of the 3×33\times 3 blue square, the rest of the table reproduces part of the table of coefficients for LG⁡(K−l)\mathrm{LG}(K_{-l}). So any relation needed to satisfy Conjecture 1.8 that does not involve any of the nine coefficients in the blue square is true by the induction hypothesis. To conclude, we need to show that all relations involving at least one of these nine coefficients are true. To do this the only way is to consider all possible cases. A useful tool here is Corollary 3.4 that reduces the study of inequalities along any line to proving the inequalities involving three consecutive coefficients, most of which are already hold by induction. We omit the remaining details of verifying the inequalities for brevity.

∎

5.4. LG\mathrm{LG} is not (denormalized) Lorentzian on alternating links for any obvious choice of variables

Here we consider various choices of variables in the presentation for the Links–Gould polynomial of the trefoil. For each choice, we exhibit a choice of derivative and corresponding quadratic form whose Hessian has more than one positive eigenvalue.

LG⁡(𝟥𝟣)​(t0,t1)\displaystyle\mathrm{LG}(\mathsf{3_{1}})(t_{0},t_{1}) =−t02​t1+t02−t0​t12+2​t0​t1−t0+t12−t1+1\displaystyle=-t_{0}^{2}t_{1}+t_{0}^{2}-t_{0}t_{1}^{2}+2t_{0}t_{1}-t_{0}+t_{1}^{2}-t_{1}+1
𝒩∘Homog⁡(LG⁡(𝟥𝟣)​(−t0,−t1))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\mathrm{LG}(\mathsf{3_{1}})(-t_{0},-t_{1})) ={12​t02​t1+12​t02​z+12​t0​t12+2​t0​t1​z+12​t0​z2+12​t12​z+12​t1​z2+13!​z3\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{matrix}\dfrac{1}{2}t_{0}^{2}t_{1}+\dfrac{1}{2}t_{0}^{2}z+\dfrac{1}{2}t_{0}t_{1}^{2}+2t_{0}t_{1}z\\[8.61108pt] +\dfrac{1}{2}t_{0}z^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}t_{1}^{2}z+\dfrac{1}{2}t_{1}z^{2}+\dfrac{1}{3!}z^{3}\end{matrix}\right.
∂∂z​[𝒩∘Homog⁡(LG⁡(𝟥𝟣)​(−t0,−t1))]\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial z}[\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\mathrm{LG}(\mathsf{3_{1}})(-t_{0},-t_{1}))] =12​t02+2​t0​t1+t0​z+12​t12+t1​z+12​z2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}t_{0}^{2}+2t_{0}t_{1}+t_{0}z+\frac{1}{2}t_{1}^{2}+t_{1}z+\frac{1}{2}z^{2}
H\displaystyle H =(121211111)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&1\\ 2&1&1\\ 1&1&1\end{pmatrix}
λ1=−1,λ2=2−3,λ3=2+3.\lambda_{1}=-1,\quad\lambda_{2}=2-\sqrt{3},\quad\lambda_{3}=2+\sqrt{3}\,.

Since this derivative has a Hessian with two positive eigenvalues, the Links–Gould polynomial is not denormalized Lorentzian.

We also consider replacing a variable with a power of itself together with a variable shift such that we obtain a polynomial.

L​G​(𝟥𝟣)​(t0,t1−1)⋅t12\displaystyle LG(\mathsf{3_{1}})(t_{0},t_{1}^{-1})\cdot t_{1}^{2} =t02​t12−t02​t1−t0​t12+2​t0​t1−t0+t12−t1+1\displaystyle=t_{0}^{2}t_{1}^{2}-t_{0}^{2}t_{1}-t_{0}t_{1}^{2}+2t_{0}t_{1}-t_{0}+t_{1}^{2}-t_{1}+1
𝒩∘Homog⁡(LG⁡(𝟥𝟣)​(t0,t1−1))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\mathrm{LG}(\mathsf{3_{1}})(t_{0},t_{1}^{-1})) ={14​t02​t12+12​t02​t1​z+12​t0​t12​z+t0​t1​z2+16​t0​z3+14​t12​z2+16​t1​z3+124​z4\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{matrix}\dfrac{1}{4}t_{0}^{2}t_{1}^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}t_{0}^{2}t_{1}z+\dfrac{1}{2}t_{0}t_{1}^{2}z+t_{0}t_{1}z^{2}\\[8.61108pt] +\dfrac{1}{6}t_{0}z^{3}+\dfrac{1}{4}t_{1}^{2}z^{2}+\dfrac{1}{6}t_{1}z^{3}+\dfrac{1}{24}z^{4}\end{matrix}\right.
∂2∂t0​∂z​[𝒩∘Homog⁡(LG⁡(𝟥𝟣)​(t0,t1−1))]\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial t_{0}\partial z}[\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\mathrm{LG}(\mathsf{3_{1}})(t_{0},t_{1}^{-1}))] =t0​t1+12​t12+2​t1​z+12​z2\displaystyle=t_{0}t_{1}+\frac{1}{2}t_{1}^{2}+2t_{1}z+\frac{1}{2}z^{2}
H\displaystyle H =(010112021)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&1&2\\ 0&2&1\end{pmatrix}
λ1=−1.39138238,λ2=0.22713444,λ3=3.16424794.\lambda_{1}=-1.39138238,\quad\lambda_{2}=0.22713444,\quad\lambda_{3}=3.16424794\,.

Another choice of variables for the Links-Gould polynomial comes from [GK]. We write this polynomial V1​(p,q)V_{1}(p,q). Then

V1,𝟥𝟣​(p,q)\displaystyle V_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(p,q) =p2​q2−p​q2−p​q+2​q+1−q​p−1−p−1+p−2\displaystyle=p^{2}q^{2}-pq^{2}-pq+2q+1-qp^{-1}-p^{-1}+p^{-2}
𝒩∘Homog⁡(p2⋅V1,𝟥𝟣​(−p,q))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(p^{2}\cdot V_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(-p,q)) ={12⋅4!​p4​q2+12⋅3!​p3​q2​z+12⋅3!​p3​q​z2+13!​p2​q​z3+12⋅4!​p2​z4+14!​p​q​z4+15!​p​z5+16!​z6\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{matrix}\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 4!}p^{4}q^{2}+\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 3!}p^{3}q^{2}z+\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 3!}p^{3}qz^{2}+\dfrac{1}{3!}p^{2}qz^{3}\\[8.61108pt] +\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 4!}p^{2}z^{4}+\dfrac{1}{4!}pqz^{4}+\dfrac{1}{5!}pz^{5}+\dfrac{1}{6!}z^{6}\end{matrix}\right.
∂4∂p3​∂z​[𝒩∘Homog⁡(p2⋅V1,𝟥𝟣​(−p,q))]\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{4}}{\partial p^{3}\partial z}[\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(p^{2}\cdot V_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(-p,q))] =p​q+q​z+12​z2\displaystyle=pq+qz+\frac{1}{2}z^{2}
H\displaystyle H =(010101011)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&1\\ 0&1&1\end{pmatrix}
λ1=−1.24698,λ2=0.445042,λ3=1.80194.\lambda_{1}=-1.24698,\quad\lambda_{2}=0.445042,\quad\lambda_{3}=1.80194\,.

There are also Conway polynomial like changes of variables for V1V_{1} which desymmetrize V1V_{1}. We denote the change of variables in u=p+p−1​q−1u=p+p^{-1}q^{-1} and qq by V~1​(u,q)\tilde{V}_{1}(u,q). We have

V~1,𝟥𝟣​(u,q)\displaystyle\tilde{V}_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(u,q) =q2​u2+(2​q3−q2+q)​u+(q4−q3+q2−q+1)\displaystyle=q^{2}u^{2}+(2q^{3}-q^{2}+q)u+(q^{4}-q^{3}+q^{2}-q+1)
𝒩∘Homog⁡(V~1,𝟥𝟣​(−u,−q))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\tilde{V}_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(-u,-q)) ={12⋅2​u2​q2+23!​u​q3+12​u​q2​z+12​u​q​z2+14!​q4+13!​q3​z+12⋅2​q2​z2+13!​q​z3+14!​z4\displaystyle=\left\{\begin{matrix}\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 2}u^{2}q^{2}+\dfrac{2}{3!}uq^{3}+\dfrac{1}{2}uq^{2}z+\dfrac{1}{2}uqz^{2}+\dfrac{1}{4!}q^{4}\\[8.61108pt] +\dfrac{1}{3!}q^{3}z+\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 2}q^{2}z^{2}+\dfrac{1}{3!}qz^{3}+\dfrac{1}{4!}z^{4}\end{matrix}\right.
∂2∂u​∂q​[𝒩∘Homog⁡(V~1,𝟥𝟣​(−u,−q))]\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial u\partial q}[\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\tilde{V}_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(-u,-q))] =u​q+q2+q​z+12​z2\displaystyle=uq+q^{2}+qz+\frac{1}{2}z^{2}
H\displaystyle H =(010121011)\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&2&1\\ 0&1&1\end{pmatrix}
λ1=−0.532089,λ2=0.652704,λ3=2.87939.\lambda_{1}=-0.532089,\quad\lambda_{2}=0.652704,\quad\lambda_{3}=2.87939\,.

We also set V^1​(v,q)\hat{V}_{1}(v,q) to be the polynomial in the variables v=p+p−1​q−1−q−q−1v=p+p^{-1}q^{-1}-q-q^{-1} and qq. Then

V^1,𝟥𝟣​(v,q)\displaystyle\hat{V}_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(v,q) =v2​q2−(q2+q)​v\displaystyle=v^{2}q^{2}-(q^{2}+q)v
𝒩∘Homog⁡(V^1,𝟥𝟣​(−v,q))\displaystyle\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\hat{V}_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(-v,q)) =12⋅2​v2​q2+12​v​q2​z+12​v​q​z2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2\cdot 2}v^{2}q^{2}+\frac{1}{2}vq^{2}z+\frac{1}{2}vqz^{2}
∂2∂v​∂q​[𝒩∘Homog⁡(V^1,𝟥𝟣​(−v,q))]\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial v\partial q}[\mathcal{N}\circ\mathrm{Homog}(\hat{V}_{1,\mathsf{3_{1}}}(-v,q))] =v​q+q​z+12​z2\displaystyle=vq+qz+\frac{1}{2}z^{2}
H=(010101011)H=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&1\\ 0&1&1\end{pmatrix}
λ1=−1.24698,λ2=0.445042,λ3=1.80194.\lambda_{1}=-1.24698,\quad\lambda_{2}=0.445042,\quad\lambda_{3}=1.80194\,.

Which is the same Hessian as LG⁡(𝟥𝟣)​(t0,t1)\mathrm{LG}(\mathsf{3_{1}})(t_{0},t_{1}).

6. Values of Links–Gould on some classes of links

We present the coefficients of the Links–Gould polynomial on (2,n)(2,n)-torus links, and on twist knots in the variables (t0,t1)(t_{0},t_{1}) and (t0−1,t1−1)(t_{0}^{-1},t_{1}^{-1}).
